newsitem.title: FRANCE: Ranariddh vows to lead resistance against Hun Sen.
newsitem.headline: Ranariddh vows to lead resistance against Hun Sen.

text.p: Cambodian First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh said on Monday his rival, Hun Sen, had ousted him and vowed to organise resistance around the world.

"We must have an emissary outside Cambodia. I have decided to be this emissary, to explain to the world what is happening in Cambodia and to ask the international community not to accept the result of this coup d'etat," he told Reuters.

Fighting broke out in the capital Phnom Penh on Saturday when Second Prime Minister Hun Sen ordered a crackdown on "illegal troops" under Ranariddh's command. But Hun Sen appeared to be in control of the capital and its outskirts on Monday.
The two men had shared power as co-heads of a fractured and unwieldy coalition government formed after a United Nations-run election in 1993.

Hun Sen had accused Ranariddh of smuggling defectors into the capital from the deadly Khmer Rouge guerrilla group, led by the mysterious and evasive Pol Pot and blamed for the deaths of more than a million Cambodians during their 1975-79 "killing fields" rule.
Ranariddh, in an interview, denied he had sought an alliance with the Khmer Rouge and accused his rival of using his contacts with the group as an excuse to stage a coup d'etat.
Ranariddh, currently in the southern French city of Aix-en-Provence, said he had fled his homeland before the fighting broke out, on the advice of his generals.

He said the generals had told him on Friday that Hun Sen was preparing a coup d'etat and warned him that if he remained in Cambodia and Hun Sen succeeded, there would be no one outside the country to plead their cause.
"It was against my heart's desire that I left my country on July 4," he said. "The generals did not want me to be captured or worse, taken hostage."

Ranariddh later told Reuters after a meeting with the Japanese ambassador, Koichiro Matsuura, and French Foreign Ministry deputy secretary general Claude Martin that he had asked their governments not to recognise the Hun Sen regime.
"This is clearly a coup d'etat staged by Hun Sen and I asked the two representatives from France and Japan not to recognise any government issued from the coup d'etat," he said.

He said he urged them to recognise the power-sharing arrangement that came out of the 1993 election supervised by the United Nations (U.N.). France and Japan would issue a statement saying they "will not accept any government issued from any illegal means," he said.

A Japanese embassy spokesman said Japan and France asked for "maintenance of the constitution, maintenance of the ceasefire and conciliation of the Cambodian people," adding that Ranariddh had agreed and asked for cooperation of France and Japan.

After a brief stay in France, Ranariddh said he plans to travel to the United States and plans meetings with the U.N. Secretary General, Koffi Annan, as well as Presidents of the General Assembly and Security Council.
He also hopes to meet the U.S. Vice-President, Al Gore, and Secretary of State Madeleine Albright. He will then go onto one of the Asian nations making up the ASEAN alliance, he said.

France is the former colonial power in Cambodia, where about 2,000 French nationals still live, according to the French Foreign Ministry. The Asian nation was a French protectorate for 90 years until independence in 1953.
